The Reintegration of Zeqawistan

The Maqami Sultanate, founded in 1002 by the legendary conqueror Sultan Maqam Dastakbar (Maqam ibn Akram), is the predecessor of Maqamistan. The territory was inhabited by heavily Persianized Arabs living in total anarchy, and Sultan Dastakbar was the one to unite the various quarreling tribes under his rule. Under the oak tree, he was blessed by the Sufi Sheikh Aqhoja of the Hojaiyya order, who prophecised that his descendants would rule the world.

Maqami armies were renowned for their diversity and discipline. In addition to Arab and Turkic units, Dastakbar's service attracted a large number of Circassian and Turkic warriors, who were prized for their loyalty and skill in combat. Sultan Dastakbar was the one to form several aspects of the Maqami military, which is often called the first standing army in West Shamat. The "Shahbaz" cavalry, which was made up of Circassians and Turks, was for centuries known as the strongest cavalry unit on the continent, if not the whole world. They were known for their mastery of the horse. The "Diwana" infantry units, whose main role was to act as front-line shock troops, were recruited solely from the mentally ill, or those judged for heavy charges like murder or rape. They were used as human shields for the proper army, and their main role was to scare and demotivate the enemy. They would dress up in unnerving, off-putting clothing and make weird sounds during battle.

The Sultanate expanded across several continents under Dastakbar and his successors. During the reign of Sultan Mikhmandar I, the empire defeated and annexed its long time rivals, the Sultanate of Selqom. This massively accelerated further conquests. Sultan Qadir was the first to invite Circassians to not only serve in Maqami armies but settle in the empire, starting a process of Circassian migration that would last centuries. Isfandiyar the Thunderbolt is known for his conquests in both the east and the west, and he had conquered vast territories in only a decade, before he died falling off his horse. Sultan Rida al-Din expanded the empire's territories into the Latin coasts, and built the massive city of Puerto Dastakbar as a key trading hub. In other cases, merchants from several Latin countries arrived along the coasts, trading goods and wealth. These Latin communities established themselves over many generations, speaking their own language and keeping their distinct identity while gradually assimilating local customs and Islam.

Sultan Abdul-Aziz I famously declared the Maqami Sultanate as the "Global State" (Arabic: al-Dawlah al-ʻĀlamīyah), stating that it does not recognize any other nations, claiming the entire planet as Maqami territory. This notion was endorsed also by sucessive sultans. Sultan Muhammad II is famous for refusing to communicate with the King of Saltaria, dismissing him as a "mere rebel leader".

Over generations, the Sultanate, emboldened by its immense power, stagnated. A confirmation of this occured in 1834 when the sultanate renounced its claim over the entire world and started establishing diplomatic relations with other nations. Some reformist sultans tried to fight the stagnation, but their reforms failed. Such as Sultan Karim the Reformer, who attempted to reform the empire, but was asassinated. In time, rise of Arab nationalism caused distability. These Arab nationalists took control of many institutions and put down other groups. Shabbabism, which was founded in the late Sultanate era by Abdul-Shabbab ibn al-Shabbab, who called himself the "Promised Light," originated from the radical wing of the Young Arabs movement. These Arab nationalists held the view that "Maqamistan is for Arabs" and deliberately undermined the Sultanate's traditional multi-ethnic character. By establishing al-Shabbab as a monotheistic deity who supposedly selected Arabs as a superior race destined to rule over all others, Shabbabism fundamentally departs from Islam while claiming to honor Islamic prophets. All prophets, including Moses and Jesus, were Arabs, according to the faith, which labels those who disagree as unbelievers. Non-Arabs are allowed to live but are never allowed to lead, according to Shabbabist philosophy.

There were many peasant revolts, protests from merchants, and uprisings in border areas. While the Sultanate still maintained a standing army, its focus on suppressing minor rebellions rather than addressing systemic corruption further alienated the population. Peasant uprisings followed by a major Circassian-Latin led revolt led to a civil war in 1979.

During the height of the civil war, Jose Velazquez, a Latin mercenary from a foreign nation, was shipwrecked on Maqami shores. He was rescued by the local Latin Maqami community, who nursed him back to health. Velazquez fully adopted Maqami culture, and even adopted the second name "Muhamed". He took up arms and started unifying neighboring villages. Over time, Velazquez emerged as a charismatic leader; his military experience, ability to deliver speeches, combined with his devotion to Islam, allowed him to unite Arabs, Circassians, and Latins under a common cause. Leading a decisive revolution, he overthrew the corrupt sultan and proclaimed the founding of the Peoples Islamic Republic of Maqamistan in 1982. Sultan Rashid was informed of his dethroning, and he said nothing, simply laughing and leaving the room. Maqamistan's economy operates under Just Order Socialism (Arabic: al-Niẓām al-ʻĀdil al-Ishtirākī), the revolutionary framework outlined in Jose "Akhi" Velazquez's The Blue Book (Arabic: al-Kitāb al-Azraq).

And that is how Maqamistan came to be.
However, this post is not about Maqamistan proper, but rather a land known as Zeqawistan.

Zeqawistan was ruled by what would later become the Global State since the 14th century, when Sultan Isfandiyar the Thunderbolts campaigns brought about the conquest of the region. Known for his swift and decisive campaigns, Isfandiyar rushed his army to Durband, the capital of Zeqawistan, imprisoned their sultan, and annexed the country overnight. The territory, strategic for its coastal holdings, had historically been home to a population of Turkic and Iranic peoples who had slowly adopted the Shia branch of Islam of the Ithna-Ashari (Twelver) denomination due to trade relations with other countries. After the conquest by the Sunni Maqami Sultanate, Shiism was tolerated but gradually assimilated, with most Shia converting to Sunni over time, to the Hanafi-Maturidi denomination championed by the sultanate.

For centuries, Zeqawistan was a province of Maqamistan, with the regional capital of Durband serving as a trade hub for spices, silks, and other goods being traded by merchants from all over the world.

The loss of Zeqawistan was truly a tragedy. As the Sultanate stagnated in the 19th century, provinces like Zeqawistan found themselves increasingly neglected by the central government in Maqam Dar-as-Salam. Local governors, initially appointed by the Sultan, began to rule with near-complete autonomy.  The final break came in 1891, when Governor Timur Qazaq declared himself Khan of Zeqawistan, formally renounced allegiance to Sultan Abdul-Hamid III, converted to Shiism and started a crackdown of the Arab-Sunni population. Within decades, the population was mostly consisted of Shiite Turks and Iranians.

The new Khanate of Zeqawistan was anything but stable. There were ethnic tensions and chaos. But above all, the economy was terrible, as without the protection of the Maqami Sultanate, trade routes fell apart and the Zeqawi economy crashed completely. After Timur Qazaq was assassinated by a Sunni, the region fell into a civil war between Turkic tribes, led by Alim Qazaq, son of Timur Qazaq, and Iranian communities, led by Alibaba Shah Bahram. The civil war was so bloody and long that after some time, both sides declared an uneasy truce, splitting the land between Iranic tribes and Turkic tribes. Zeqawistan was, by all means, a mess.

During the Maqami Civil War (1979-1982), both sides in Zeqawistan remained neutral, with Khan Ömürtaq refusing to take sides and Shah Rustam only nominally supporting the rebellion. Many Zeqawis, however, watched the revolution with interest. 

The Blue Books message resonated with many Zeqawis, Iranic and Turkic alike. Pan-Zeqawi intellectuals who supported the unification of Zeqawistan were inspired by Just Order ideology of the Blue Book, and started advocating for it. After Maqamistan was established, Maqami intelligence agency supported people like this. Over time, underground study circles formed all over Zeqawistan, infiltrating politics, tribal meetings, universities and mosques, discussing Just Order Socialism and debating whether similar principles could save Zeqawistan.

By the early 1980s, both the Khan and the Shah governments were notorious for their corruption, their rich elite, and the poor commoners. The civil war re-ignited briefly, with both sides going to war, but a truce was declared after a few months. The neighboring powerhouse of Celia started questioning Zeqawi independence, preparing for an intervention, which radicalized the people even more.

In March 1985, a huge protest erupted in the Iranian Zeqawi capital Durband, followed by similar protests in the Turkic capital of Ötlebaliq. The governments tried to put down the rebellions with bloody force, which only radicalized the protestors. Terrified to lose their power, the Turkic and Iranic sides quickly signed an alliance, entering into a confederation of United Zeqawistan. The unity of Zeqawistan, a dream of centuries, was only fulfilled so that the people could be oppressed further, rather ironic.

When soldiers from the predominantly Iranic 5th Infantry Division refused orders to fire on protestors and instead joined them, the regime's fate was sealed for real.

On April 19, 1985, the rulers of Zeqawistan fled the country, leaving behind a power vacuum. The people raided the government buildings, the palaces. The Zeqawi Peoples Assembly was established. After some conferences, they the formation of a provisional government: Peoples Islamic Republic of Zeqawistan. A referendum was held, with 98% voting to join Maqamistan, albeit the results were rather suspicious.

Maqamistan accepted, of course. Maqami armies took control of Durband and Ötlebaliq within days. President Abu Muammar al-Selqawi and Prime Minister Jose Akhi Velazquez met with representatives from Zeqawistan  in June 1985 to discuss things further. Neighboring countries were also part of the discussions. No one knew if he was joking when Velazquez argued that Zeqawistan must join Maqamistan because the names rhyme, si?

Zeqawi demands were simple, most chief of which an autonomous region where Turkic and Iranic languages were recognized. After much thought, this was accepted by Maqamistan. The Durband Accords, signed December 1985, established Zeqawistan as an autonomous zone within Maqamistan.

Maqamistan poured resources into integrating and rebuilding Zeqawistan. Investments into infrastructure, establishing schools and hospitals, organizing workers' cooperatives. The Antcoin replaced the worthless Zeqawi dinar. The Blue Book was translated into both Zeqawi Turkic and Zeqawi Persian dialects and distributed widely; Known as the Kök Kitab and the Ketāb-e Ābī. By 1987, Zeqawistan's economy had stabilized and even begun growing. The riba-free banking system was established, following Sharia principles as interpreted in Just Order Socialism.  There were ethnic tensions, as expected, but they were handled by the government.

Political change proved much more difficult. The establishment of Just Order Socialism faced resistance from traditional power structures. Tribal leaders, particularly among the Turkic population (known as agha-mirza), worried about losing influence. Some Muslim groups, both Turkic and Iranic, opposed socialism altogether. Some Iranic atheistic intellectuals, while supportive of socialism, questioned whether Islamic principles should govern economic policy. 

In 1988, tribal leaders in the rural Eltemek region launched a full-scale rebellion, declaring the short-lived Khanate of Eltemek. The Maqami response was violent and brutal, but swift.

After the rebellion was crushed, Akhi Velazquez personally travelled the Eltemek and met with tribal elders for weeks. A compromise was reached. Within Turkic regions of Zeqawistan, traditional Turkic pastoral nomadism was recognized as a form of "folk socialism", thus compatible with Just Order principles. Basically, almost full autonomy was granted.

The formal ceremony of reunification took place on September 16, 1992. "We respect our ancestors, by the grace of God, for they had protected peoples rights But The Global State is no more. Perhaps it was an arrogant dream of conquest," Velazquez said, "But the Just Order is a humble reality."

The integration of Zeqawistan boosted the economy of Maqamistan. Trade power increased, and the agricultural power of the new province still offers a lot of potential, yet to be exploited.

When the rulers of Zeqawistan fled on April 25, 1985, they believed distance would grant them safety. They were wrong.

Khan Ömürtaq Qazaq, the Turkic ruler, escaped to [nation]Nordiheim[/nation] with his family and a convoy of loyal guards, carrying with them anything they could loot from the treasury. Goods stolen from the people Classic opressors, right?

He settled in a big city under the false identity of "Omar Qazi," pretending to be a wealthy merchant. Some reports suggest a certain vacuum cleaner salesman was involved in the creation of this fake identity...

For three years, he lived in a villa, believing that he got away with this crimes, that he would be forgotten. 

But God does not forget. And neither does Maqamistan. Do not think that God is unaware of what the opressors do That is a verse from the Quran in the chapter of Ibrahim. Thus this operation was codenamed Operation Ibrahim.

On the night of November 16, 1988, Ömürtaq Omar Qazi hosted a dinner party for local businessmen and elites, hoping to push his new identity. 

A pretty lady, the daughter of a prominent family, appareantly, was his companion for the night. He was a bit too drunk to be suspicious. She was pretty and playful, just as he liked. As he stepped onto his balcony to smoke, a single silenced shot killed him instantly. His body was found in the balcony hours later.

Publicly, the Nordiheim police investigated briefly, but the case went cold within weeks. In reality, Nordiheim was made aware of this operation weeks ago. The pretty lady in question was Maqami spy all along, Laura Iglecias. Everything was planned.

The second part of Operation Ibrahim was not much different.

Shah Rustam Bahram, the Iranic co-ruler, had fled to [nation]Baladullah[/nation]. Unlike Ömürtaq, who at least tried to blend in, Rustam was arrogant. He believed his connections would protect him. He kept publicly living his lavish lifestyle as if he were still royalty.

Maqami intelligence had been tracking him since the day he fled. When Maqamistan reached out to Baladullah with evidence of Rustam's crimes, they were allowed to continue with the operation. The operation was kept secret from the public on both sides.

Rustam's mistake was routine. Every Friday, he attended prayers at a local mosque, in lavish clothes, showing off how religious and pious he is, reasserting his claim for Zeqawistan.

On March 9, 1989, as Rustam's convoy returned from Friday prayers, it was ambushed on a quiet road outside the city. A Maqami operative, Madina Shalaqo, approached Rustam's vehicle and delivered two precise shots through the window.

Rustam died before he realized what was going on. No arrests were made.

[/spoiler]
